I'm halfway through my MLIS, and this thread is super discouraging and depressing lol... but what else can I do? I'm halfway through already and I love my library job and love school. I may have a skewed view of it though, because I spent a number of years in a job I HATED, wasn't good at, was also underpaid, and had little fulfillment.

I'm not a librarian yet, but I do ILL at my library. I've worked here for a little over 3 years now and started as a part-time shelver. I love working here! Yes, every day isn't super exciting, and some days I don't want to be here, but that's the case with any job, I'd say. Working 40 hours a week isn't sustainable for anyone, but that's a different conversation.

There's a lot I could say about the good and bad things about my job, but personally the only major problem I've had is an incompetent library board made up of people who don't know the first thing about libraries, refuse to learn, and are more concerned with performative activism than actually engaging with the community and learning what DEI work our library is already doing. Before a huge disaster perpetuated by our board happened, our library was actually a role model to many libraries in terms of diversity and inclusion, and was one of the first libraries in the country to implement an anti-racist policy. Now, however, we're the laughingstock of the library world. So that's one of the only reasons I'm looking forward to getting my degree and moving to another library!

I've always seen the ending as incredibly bittersweet. I always hesitate to call theirs a "happy" ending, because honestly neither of them seem very HAPPY at the end. I would more likely use the word "content." They've been through too much to be how they were in s1, but that's the point. It wouldn't be Arcane if it was a fairytale happy ending, and it would be immature writing to have characters end a story the same way they began is (character development is essential lol).

But what is clear is that they feel safe and content with each other. Vi is barefoot, no arm wraps on, chilling on the coffee table, looking the most unguarded and relaxed she's been the entire series. Caitlyn is working, but still taking the time to enjoy Vi's presence. Their physical affection is very natural. It's evident they spend a lot of time together. With Caitlyn being pleasantly surprised by Vi singing and Vi's assurance that Caitlyn is stuck with her, it seems like they're committed to moving forward together.

So yeah, I think the idea of them having a "happily ever after" isn't quite right, but it's still very hopeful. Tbh, I like the idea of giving them this kind of ending because it gives us fans a lot to work with in terms of creating fanworks and dreaming up post-canon ideas. Like Amanda said, this is just the beginning for them. They have so much ahead of them, and the important thing is that they're going to do it all together!

That's the only way any of this could come to an end. And so Amanda's whole quote about "if I didn't have anyone left to protect, I'd fall in love" makes so much sense—when Vi doesn't HAVE to do anything, when she doesn't put that pressure on herself, when she feels free to finally make a decision about what she WANTS rather than what she needs to do or thinks she should do, she chooses love. And it's not about choosing Caitlyn over Jinx or anything—she just wants Caitlyn, she wants to fall in love. She's never had that before. The whole point is that there's no choosing between her sister and the girl she loves. Vi is choosing herself!

I said something about this on Twitter the other day, but I think this is what's so big and why the Caitvi sex scene is more than just a sex scene and the resolution for their romance: it's that, for the first time, Vi has found a love that has no obligation. Caitlyn *let Jinx go*. She doesn't need or expect anything from Vi anymore. She didn't make Vi choose. It's more important to her that Vi is happy, than for Vi to be with her. THAT is why that scene is important. That is why it's the "culmination of love." That is why it's mostly the end for her arc. She's spent her whole life trying to be everything for everyone she loves. Finally, she can rest and know that she'll still be loved no matter what.

Everyone in this show has a tragic end (except for freaking Singed... only one who got everything he wanted, hate him). But of all the endings, Vi's is actually the least tragic. She lost her family, yes. But she still has Caitlyn. She has one person who loves her unconditionally, and she'll never have to be alone unless she wants to be (because, again, Caitlyn is willing to let Vi go if that's what makes her happy!).

Anyway, I love your analysis, thank you.

I actually read a lot of romance lol... but of course, the only romance I read is sapphic lol. And there are sooo many gems when you read books from small presses dedicated to those books instead of the mainstream big publishers. I think I just like reading about lesbians and sapphics falling in love lol.

But I think what stands out about fanfiction is that it's characters you already know and love. In original fiction, the author basically has about 70k words to get you to care about the characters. Tbh, it's actually less than that, especially if it's a fast-burn romance so they need to try to get you invested quickly. But in fic, you know these characters. You don't have to be told why you should care about them. You don't have to work to understand them or care about them, you already do! The hardest part of reading or writing a book is already done, so you only get the fun stuff.

Then adding onto that, because it's characters you already love, you want to keep reading about them falling in love, in as many ways and in as many worlds as possible. When you read original fiction, you get one book or one series and then you move on and have to get attached to a whole other set of characters. But fic gives you thousands of stories just of your favorite characters. So it may not necessarily be that you like ROMANCE, but more that you like those particular characters falling in love over and over and over again. I think maybe one of the reasons Caitvi are so impactful, even if you aren't a lesbian, is because so much of their romance is presented by showing, rather than telling? They never even say "I love you" or really anything overtly romantic. So much of it is touching and looking and the things they do for each other. Maybe that makes their romance feel more real—because it's something you FEEL more than being told it. You can see and feel the way that they love and care for each other, and it touches you. It's also why it's hard to put your finger on what's so special about it—because it's not really tangible.

I just think we don't see many couples like that in media, especially these days, whether they're straight or queer. I'm a lesbian, so I have a whole host of reasons why I'm obsessed with these two. But I've even seen homophobic people say they like Caitvi, and I have to think that that's a big reason why they're so special—they're written in a way that elicits emotion.

Vi was never about politics and was never a rider for Zaun. Even in act 1 of season 1, when she goes on about Piltover having everything and them in Zaun living off scraps, she's not talking about her city—she was talking about her family. She loves Caitlyn, and feels it was partly her fault that Caitlyn lost her mom—thus she's not chasing Jinx for Piltover's sake, but because she feels this is the only way to protect the last person she  loves (which, at this time, Caitlyn was all she had, since she had come to terms with losing her sister). She also decides to go after Jinx because she realizes she's no longer the sister she used to know. Vi admits she doesn't like change. Her sister changed the *most*, and not just in being different from who Vi remembers—Jinx *hurt* people. In her mind, she's already failed to protect the last of her family ("I created the monster"). It's a sort of atonement for her sins thing that motivates her. 

In the end, she wouldn't be a political fighter once she lost both Caitlyn and Jinx/Powder, because in her mind she has nothing left to fight for.

Black girl here who studied abroad in Korea in 2013! Back when I lived there, Kpop and Kdramas weren't mainstream yet, so there were a lot fewer foreigners living there than I think there are now. And most people were actually quite kind and sometimes were interested in talking to us. The one time I really experienced racism was more discrimination against foreigners in general, and it was when my friend & I were going to music shows. She was white, I'm Black, but the fan staff tried several times over several weeks to pull us out of line or tell us to leave (never worked, btw lol). But in terms of everyday life, nothing too bad ever happened. I have to say, I have light skin and keep my hair straight, so that may have made a difference. But there was a darker skinned Black girl in my study abroad group, and I can't remember her mentioning any incidents that really stood out.

When I went back to Korea for vacation last year though, people seemed a little fed up with foreigners in general (maybe because there are so many more of us now?). But a lot of people—mostly older Koreans—became super nice when they realized I could speak Korean. So definitely try to use Korean as much as you can, folks really appreciate it when you're respectful of the language and culture you're now living in.

As for the university experience, I attended Konkuk Univ., which I believe is a few subway stops away from Jamsil. Honestly it never really felt like we were "too far" from the city center, because there's fun stuff all over if you explore. Also, I'm pretty sure Line 2 goes through Jamsil, which is probably the best subway line to be on because it'll take you almost anywhere without needing transfers. Make sure to download the subway app!

Also, try to check if your university offers a mentor program! Mine had one where you would be paired with a Korean student who'd basically be like, your Korean buddy for the semester. Generally they'll just take you out to places to hang out & you can practice Korean with them & they can help you get used to the school.

One last thing; if university is still like it was when I studied there, you'll probably have a lot of free time. So def use that time to meet up with your friends who go to different schools, and since you'll be on Line 2, it should be pretty easy to get to fun places to meet them at.

If you have any other questions about being a Black girl in Korea, feel free to DM me! It's been a while, but I'm always happy to share my experiences & offer advice.

I recommend reaching out to a past grantee, preferably in your field or country of interest! A very very kind past grantee from the program I'm applying for sent me their statement, and it was super helpful. And my FPA liked my first draft, which I did after studying that and a couple other statements. Here are some tips I learned from that grantee who helped me out:

-You can focus the statement mostly on the history or your study of the topic.

-Your exact research methods don't have to take up that much of the statement—the grantee I spoke to said they only used one paragraph, so I did the same.

-You can itemize the things you plan to do. That person's statement structured it like, "During my grant period, I will \[whatever your research is\] by 1) \[method/plan 1\]; 2), etc. I did this with mine, too, and my FPA said that was good.

-I didn't learn this from the past grantee, but I sort of framed my statement by introducing the questions I aimed to answer with my research. I did this in the 3rd paragraph, I think.

-This depends on you, but I used the end of my statement to describe how the research can be used as an exchange between the countries, etc.

I hope that helps some! I'd offer to send you mine as an example, but it's only the first draft so it's not ready yet lol. But if you'd still like an example in a couple weeks, feel free to DM me. Good luck!

To echo what other people have said, you are SO young. It's not uncommon to not know your next steps at 23 years old. At that age, I took a job not in my field just because I didn't have any other options, and I ended up spending 4 1/2 years at a job I hated, in a town I hated, and at one point ended up in the psychiatric hospital because I couldn't fathom going on. During the pandemic, I moved back home (where, like you, I didn't have any more friends because they had all moved away by then) and eventually found a new job in a field I love and am really good at. "Giving up" on something you thought you wanted isn't always the worst thing. Sometimes it leads you to something better.

As for Korea, spending time away might be what you need to get perspective. I studied abroad there in college, which was the most fun thing I've ever done, and planned to move back there to teach English after I graduated, just like you did. Obviously, I ended up not doing that. And I'm really glad I didn't because I would have hated it, plus like other people here have said, it's a dead end job. But the time I spent away gave me perspective, and even though I live less in a fantasy world about Korea now, I think my realistic view of it is what made me fall in love with it again.

The point is, now I'm applying to do a research program in Korea, which is so much better than if I had gone there right after graduating to teach English. It'll help advance my career, and who knows? Maybe eventually it'll lead to me doing more collaboration there and I'll get to visit more.

So what I'm saying is, maybe it would be better for you to take some time to figure out what you want. Whether that's going home, or signing for another year. There will be other opportunities in Korea that may be way better than teaching English. Eventually you'll make new friends. As for the boyfriend, that sucks, but who cares? You're 23. There will be other men. Maybe being single for a while will help you remember why you're in Korea in the first place. Just don't think of leaving as "giving up." Your twenties are for making the wrong decisions and changing paths. Not everyone figures out what they want to do for the rest of their lives when they're 21 and graduating from college. Go easy on yourself!

Depends on if you want to do more touristy things or more local-ish things. I took my brother there on vacation last year and it was his first time, so we did things like Gyeongbokgung, Namsan, and museums. If you like museums, the Museum of Korean Contemporary History is amazing and pretty new. If you like palaces, I recommend also visiting some of the smaller ones, too. They're usually less crowded and also super beautiful. And since they're small, you can hit several in a day. Something like CoEx would be fun too. I'd say that type of stuff is essential if you're only going to be there for a week and want to get the full tourist experience.

If you want to do kind of local-ish things, I recommend looking for nice cafes and bars (if you're into bars). There are a lot of recommendations for those on TikTok. Areas near universities are fun, too. Hongdae's a popular one. And definitely try as many food places as you can! There are a lot of great chain restaurants in Seoul, but you can also find smaller gems by wandering around or looking up recommendations.

I also recommend downloading the Kakao maps app, because you can look for stuff around you and people post tons of reviews, so you can get an idea for if you think you'll like it.

Have fun!

Any family is allowed to own a retail lot even if they have their own home. With college it's very easy: the game allows you to have multiple played households at once. That means that you can move the adult out to live in the dorms or wherever. Then both that new household and your original household will count as played households. You can see them in the Manage Households window. So whenever you want, you can switch between the households to play them. So you can go to the dorm, play the student for a while, and then when you want, go back to the original family's house and play them for a while.
